enterprises.name: Oil palm
enterprises.description: The dominant plantation crop in Sarawak. High yielding and mechanisable, but thirsty and intolerant of waterlogging at the root collar.
enterprises.farmerNote: A 25-year commitment. Yield responds strongly to rainfall in the driest months, so a site that is fine in an average year can still disappoint in a run of dry ones. Avoid deep peat unless you can hold the water table steady: drained peat subsides about 5 cm a year and takes the palms down with it.
sourceReferences: Corley & Tinker (2016), The Oil Palm, 5th ed.

requirements.notes: Above 500 m cooler nights slow bunch development and oil extraction rate falls.
Standing water at the collar for more than a few days kills young palms outright.

Built-up land and open water are excluded permanently. Tree cover is NOT excluded: MODIS at 500 m cannot tell an established plantation from intact forest, and 94% of this district reads as tree canopy, so excluding it would mark almost everywhere permanently unsuitable. Cells under canopy are flagged for a ground check instead.
Deep peat is plantable but subsides when drained, and is a major carbon store.
Below 100 mm a month the palm closes stomata and aborts bunches; the loss shows up in yield 20-24 months later.
Above 25% harvesting and fruit evacuation become dangerous and erosion is severe.

enterprises.name: Rubber
enterprises.description: Tapped for latex over a 25-30 year stand. More tolerant of poor acid soils than oil palm and far less demanding of capital.
enterprises.farmerNote: Tapping stops when it rains, so a very wet site costs you tapping days even though the trees grow well. Latex flows best in the cool early morning. Wind is the main physical risk: a mature stand snaps in a squall on an exposed ridge.

requirements.notes: Rubber performs poorly on peat; root anchorage is inadequate.
Mature rubber is brittle; branch snap on exposed sites is the commonest cause of stand loss.

enterprises.name: Black pepper
enterprises.description: Sarawak's signature smallholder crop and the state's highest-value perennial per hectare. Grown on posts, intensively managed, and acutely sensitive to drainage.
enterprises.farmerNote: Pepper dies from its feet. Phytophthora foot rot follows standing water, and a single wet season on a flat, poorly drained site can take out a whole garden that took three years to establish. This is the one crop where a gentle slope is an advantage rather than a nuisance.
sourceReferences: Malaysian Pepper Board, Pepper Production Technology in Malaysia

requirements.notes: The single most important factor. Foot rot follows waterlogging.
Peat holds water at the root collar; unsuitable without raised beds.
A dry spell at flowering causes spike shedding.
Persistently saturated air raises foliar disease pressure.
Unusually, flat ground scores badly: the vine needs surface water to leave quickly.
Hollows where water concentrates are where the garden dies first.

enterprises.name: Coconut
enterprises.description: Long-lived, low-input palm that tolerates sandy and saline coastal soils better than any other tree crop grown here.
enterprises.farmerNote: Forgiving of poor soil and salt, much less forgiving of shade and cold. It will stand on ground too sandy for anything else, and a brackish water table does not trouble it.

requirements.notes: Among the few crops that genuinely prefer a sandy profile.
Coconut is intolerant of shade and dull skies.
Nut set falls away below 20 C.

enterprises.name: Sago palm
enterprises.description: A starch palm of freshwater swamp and deep peat. Sarawak is the world's largest exporter, and sago is the one commercial crop that actively prefers the land everything else rejects.
enterprises.farmerNote: If your land floods and sits on peat, this is the crop that was waiting for it. Sago asks for no drainage, no bunding and almost no input; it simply needs water and time. The trade-off is patience: around ten years to first harvest.
sourceReferences: Flach (1997), Sago Palm, Promoting the Conservation and Use of Underutilized Crops 13

requirements.notes: Seasonal flooding is tolerated and even beneficial.

Herbaceous wetland is acceptable here, unlike for most crops. Built-up land and open water are excluded permanently. Tree cover is NOT excluded: MODIS at 500 m cannot tell an established plantation from intact forest, and 94% of this district reads as tree canopy, so excluding it would mark almost everywhere permanently unsuitable. Cells under canopy are flagged for a ground check instead.
Grows on deep peat without drainage, which keeps the carbon in the ground.
Sago has no drought strategy; it relies on a water table that never drops.
Needs flat ground that holds water.
Poorly drained ground is an advantage here.
Tolerates the strong acidity of undrained peat.
Wants the hollows other crops avoid.

enterprises.name: Cocoa
enterprises.description: An understorey tree that needs shade, shelter and deep, well-drained soil. Suits a mixed smallholding better than an open plantation.
enterprises.farmerNote: Cocoa dislikes wind and full exposure; it evolved under a canopy. Intercropping under thinned forest or established coconut usually works better than clearing a block for it.

requirements.notes: Shallow rooted and very drought sensitive.

enterprises.name: Durian
enterprises.description: High-value fruit tree with a long establishment and a strong premium for quality. Demands deep, freely drained soil and shelter from wind.
enterprises.farmerNote: The return is excellent and the wait is long: seven years or more before a worthwhile crop. Root rot on heavy wet soil is the usual killer, and a mature tree on a windy ridge will lose fruit before you can harvest it.

requirements.notes: Phytophthora root rot after waterlogging is the main cause of tree death.
A short dry period actually helps trigger flowering.

enterprises.name: Banana
enterprises.description: Fast to first harvest and ratoons for several years. A useful cash bridge while slower perennials establish.
enterprises.farmerNote: Fruiting within about a year makes banana the usual way to earn something from a block while the durian or pepper is still growing. It is thirsty and shallow rooted, so it suffers quickly in a dry spell, and a laden plant blows over in a squall.

requirements.notes: Shallow roots and a large leaf area make banana one of the first crops to wilt.
A bunched plant topples easily.

enterprises.name: Wet paddy
enterprises.description: Transplanted rice grown in bunded, puddled fields under standing water. The staple system of the Batang Lupar floodplain.
enterprises.farmerNote: This is the one crop that wants the low, flat, heavy ground everything else complains about. What it cannot take is heat at flowering: above about 35 C the grain simply does not fill, and you get a field that looks fine and threshes to nothing.
sourceReferences: Jagadish et al. (2007), High temperature stress and spikelet fertility in rice

requirements.notes: Seasonal inundation is wanted; only deep or flash flooding is damaging.
A dry spell at panicle initiation costs the whole season.
Acid sulphate and deep peat soils need careful water management.
The wet window has to be deep enough to establish the crop.
Bunded basins must hold an even depth of water; above 2% the earthworks stop being worth it.
Clay is what lets a puddled field hold water; a sandy field drains away faster than you can flood it.
Poor natural drainage is an asset for wet paddy.
Spikelet sterility rises steeply above 35 C during flowering.
Water concentrating here is the point, not a problem.

rotationRules.reason: Flooded paddy after flooded paddy is not a mistake. Standing water starves the soil fungi that make continuous upland cropping fail, and the floodwater grows its own nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. It is one of the few monocultures that holds up.
rotationRules.source: IRRI long-term continuous-rice experiments have run double and triple rice on the same ground for decades without yield collapse.

rotationRules.reason: Flooding changes a field's nitrogen chemistry. Most of what a legume leaves is lost once the soil goes anaerobic, and the floodwater fixes its own nitrogen anyway. A legume before wet paddy is not a mistake; it simply is not the credit it would be before maize.
rotationRules.source: Residue nitrogen mineralised before flooding is largely lost to denitrification; biological fixation in floodwater supplies a standing part of lowland rice nitrogen.

enterprises.name: Hill paddy
enterprises.description: Rainfed upland rice grown on slopes without bunding or standing water. The traditional system of the interior, still widely grown for household rice.
enterprises.farmerNote: No earthworks and no irrigation, so the rain has to arrive on time and keep coming. Yields are well below wet paddy, but the land costs nothing to prepare and the rice is grown where no sawah could be built.

requirements.notes: Upland rice has no flood tolerance.
Entirely rainfed, so a gap in the rains is a failed crop.
An unreliable year is worse here than a dry average.
Grown on slopes, but above 25% erosion under a bare seedbed becomes serious.
The soil is the only reservoir this crop has.

rotationRules.reason: Blast is the disease that decides an upland rice crop, and it carries over in stubble and volunteers. Upland rice is rotated for this reason wherever it is grown seriously.
rotationRules.source: Pyricularia oryzae pressure is far higher in aerobic upland rice than in flooded systems, and survives between crops on residue.

rotationRules.reason: Puddling destroys the soil crumb on purpose and leaves a plough pan under it. That is what holds water for paddy and what an upland crop's roots then have to get through. Give the ground a season to dry and structure itself, or break the pan first.
rotationRules.source: Puddling for lowland rice disperses aggregates and forms a compacted subsurface layer; following upland crops are well documented to suffer poor aeration and restricted rooting.

rotationRules.reason: Groundnut leaves the most of the three. The haulm stays on the field, the nodules are shed into the top soil, and the crop before this one is why the next cereal needs less fertiliser.
rotationRules.source: Groundnut residue nitrogen contributions to a following cereal are commonly reported in the 30-60 kg N/ha range where haulms are returned rather than removed for fodder.

rotationRules.reason: Soybean fixes well and then exports most of it in the grain, which is the point of growing it. What is left is the residue and the roots, and that is still worth having under the next crop.
rotationRules.source: Soybean nitrogen harvest index is high, so the net soil balance is modest even where fixation is large.

rotationRules.reason: A green manure keeps everything it fixes, because nothing leaves the field in a sack. Chopped and turned in at flowering it is the largest single nitrogen credit in this catalogue, and the reason the season it costs can be worth paying.
rotationRules.source: Crotalaria juncea incorporated at flowering commonly supplies 60-120 kg N/ha to a following crop where biomass is 4-8 t DM/ha.

rotationRules.reason: More biomass than anything else here and roots that go deeper than any annual, so it feeds the next crop and opens the ground for it at the same time. It holds the field for three to five months to do it.
rotationRules.source: Mucuna pruriens green manure is widely reported at 5-12 t DM/ha with nitrogen contributions above 100 kg/ha in humid tropical systems.

rotationRules.reason: Long bean is picked over months and pulled at the end, so less is left behind than a grain legume cut once. The credit is real and small; it is not a reason to grow it, but it is a reason to put the hungry crop behind it rather than in front.
rotationRules.source: Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis grown for repeated green pod harvest returns less residue nitrogen than a grain legume.

enterprises.name: Maize
enterprises.description: Fast, mechanisable cereal for grain or fodder. A useful rotation break after rice and a feed source for on-farm livestock.
enterprises.farmerNote: Maize will not stand wet feet for even a day or two, so it needs the drier, better-drained half of a holding. It pairs well with a legume before it, which leaves nitrogen behind.

requirements.notes: Drought at silking is the single most damaging event for maize.
Maize is notably sensitive to aluminium toxicity below pH 5.

rotationRules.reason: Continuous cereals draw nitrogen from the same depth and let stem borer and fall armyworm carry straight over. Armyworm has been resident in Malaysia since 2019 and does not need to re-arrive.
rotationRules.source: Spodoptera frugiperda was first confirmed in Peninsular Malaysia in 2019 and is now established; continuous maize is its best host.

enterprises.name: Groundnut
enterprises.description: Nitrogen-fixing legume that does well on lighter soils. One of the best rotation breaks available before a cereal.
enterprises.farmerNote: Leaves 40-60 kg of nitrogen per hectare behind for the next crop, which is why it is worth putting in ahead of maize or paddy even when the nut price is ordinary. Needs loose soil for the pegs to enter.

requirements.notes: Very wet conditions at harvest promote aflatoxin.
Calcium supply at pod fill matters as much as pH itself.
Pegs cannot penetrate a heavy clay to set pods.

rotationRules.reason: Legume after legume builds southern stem rot and root-knot nematode, and the nitrogen a legume leaves is of no use to the next legume, which fixes its own.
rotationRules.source: Sclerotium rolfsii sclerotia persist in soil and have a very wide host range; groundnut and soybean are both good hosts.

enterprises.name: Soybean
enterprises.description: Nitrogen-fixing grain legume, useful as a short rotation break and a protein source for on-farm feed.
enterprises.farmerNote: Less tolerant of acid soil than groundnut and needs the right rhizobium inoculant to fix nitrogen properly. Worth testing on a small block before committing a field.

enterprises.name: Sunn hemp
enterprises.description: Fast-growing legume green manure, cut and turned in at flowering rather than harvested. Fixes nitrogen, smothers weeds and knocks back root-knot nematode.
enterprises.farmerNote: Nothing comes off this field. What it is worth is the crop after it: six to eight weeks to flowering, then chop and turn it in while it is still soft. Leave it to set seed and it goes woody, the nitrogen locks up in the stems, and it can volunteer in the next crop. Do not let stock graze it freely — the seed is toxic to livestock.
sourceReferences: Wang et al. (2002), Crotalaria as a cover crop for nematode management

requirements.notes: Will not take standing water at any growth stage.
One of the few things in this catalogue that will sit through a dry spell.
Drought tolerant once established; the risk here is the wet end, not the dry one.
Often planted on ground too steep to crop, to hold it together.
More forgiving of acid ground than the grain legumes.

enterprises.name: Velvet bean
enterprises.description: Vigorous legume cover with the deepest roots and the most biomass in this catalogue. Grown to rebuild a tired or compacted field rather than for anything taken off it.
enterprises.farmerNote: This is the one for ground that has been cropped hard or packed down — the roots get through a pan that an annual crop cannot. It holds the field for three to five months, so it costs a real season, and it will climb anything it reaches. The beans need long soaking and boiling before anyone or anything eats them.
sourceReferences: Malaysian plantation practice for legume cover establishment

requirements.notes: Rots rather than grows where water stands.
Among the most acid-tolerant legumes grown here.

enterprises.name: Water spinach
enterprises.description: The fastest and most forgiving leafy green grown here. Cut-and-come-again for several harvests from one planting.
enterprises.farmerNote: Ready in three to four weeks and genuinely likes wet ground, so it suits the low corner of a holding that drowns everything else. The quickest way to get cash flow out of land while a perennial establishes.

requirements.notes: Semi-aquatic; tolerates and even prefers a damp hollow.

rotationRules.reason: White rust and the leaf-feeding caterpillars that live on water spinach carry straight over to the next planting, which on a three-week crop is only three weeks away.
rotationRules.source: Albugo ipomoeae-aquaticae is the main foliar disease of kangkung in South-East Asia and persists on volunteer plants and debris.

enterprises.name: Mustard greens
enterprises.description: Quick brassica leaf crop, harvested about six weeks after sowing. A market staple.
enterprises.farmerNote: Fast and reliable, but do not follow one brassica with another: club root and diamondback moth build up in the soil and in the neighbourhood. Leave at least two seasons between them.

requirements.notes: Club root is far worse on acid soil; liming is the standard control.
Heat makes the leaf bitter and brings on early bolting.

rotationRules.reason: Club root resting spores stay alive in the soil for years and build quickly under repeated brassicas. Three seasons is the longest break a four-season plan can show; the organism outlasts it.
rotationRules.source: Plasmodiophora brassicae resting spores are commonly cited as viable for seven years or more, with a soil half-life of about four.

enterprises.name: Tomato
enterprises.description: High-value fruiting vegetable, demanding in both management and drainage. Usually staked and often grown under a rain shelter here.
enterprises.farmerNote: The best margin of any vegetable on this list and the most ways to lose it. Bacterial wilt is endemic in the humid lowlands and lives in the soil, so never follow tomato with chilli, eggplant or potato. Persistent leaf wetness brings late blight.

requirements.notes: Heavy rain splits fruit and spreads soil-borne disease.
High humidity drives late blight and bacterial spot.
Pollen is sterile above about 35 C, so flowers set no fruit.

rotationRules.reason: Bacterial wilt and root-knot nematode persist in the soil for years, and tomato, chilli, eggplant and potato all feed the same organisms. This is the one pairing the planner refuses outright.
rotationRules.source: Ralstonia solanacearum race 1 has a wide solanaceous host range and survives in soil and plant debris; three to four seasons is the usual rotation advice for the tropics.

rotationRules.reason: A cereal season starves root-knot nematode. Maize and paddy are poor hosts, so the population falls while they stand, and the crop behind them starts from a lower count.
rotationRules.source: Cereals are standard rotation partners for Meloidogyne management in vegetable systems; flooding adds a second mechanism.

rotationRules.reason: Root-knot nematode does not care about plant families. Tomato, chilli, okra and cucumber are all good hosts, so following one with another keeps the population climbing even though the rotation looks varied on paper.
rotationRules.source: Meloidogyne incognita and M. javanica have host ranges spanning most tropical vegetable families; both are widespread in South-East Asian vegetable soils.

enterprises.name: Cucumber
enterprises.description: Fast trellised vine, harvested from about six weeks. Reliable local market crop.
enterprises.farmerNote: Quick and thirsty. The fruit is mostly water, so an interruption to the supply shows up immediately as bitter, misshapen cucumbers rather than as a wilted plant.

rotationRules.reason: Gummy stem blight and Fusarium carry over in cucurbit debris, and the family feeds root-knot nematode well.
rotationRules.source: Didymella bryoniae survives on crop residue; Fusarium oxysporum formae speciales are host-specific and soil-persistent.

enterprises.name: Long bean
enterprises.description: Climbing legume picked over many weeks. Fixes nitrogen while it crops, which is rare among vegetables.
enterprises.farmerNote: Earns while it improves the soil: you pick beans for two months and still leave nitrogen behind. One of the best things to put between two hungry crops.

rotationRules.reason: Legume after legume builds southern stem rot and root-knot nematode, and the nitrogen a legume leaves is of no use to the next legume, which fixes its own.

enterprises.name: Okra
enterprises.description: Heat-tolerant fruiting vegetable with a long picking window. One of the few vegetables that shrugs off a hot, humid spell.
enterprises.farmerNote: When the weather is too hot for tomato to set fruit, okra keeps going. Worth keeping in the rotation as the hot-season option, and it tolerates a wider range of soil than most.

requirements.notes: Genuinely heat tolerant; this rarely binds.

rotationRules.reason: Okra is one of the strongest root-knot nematode hosts grown here. Two okra crops running multiplies the population rather than holding it.
rotationRules.source: Abelmoschus esculentus is rated a highly susceptible host of Meloidogyne incognita in standard host-range tables.

enterprises.name: Tilapia
enterprises.description: The workhorse pond fish: fast growing, hardy, eats almost anything, and sells readily. Reaches table size in about six months.
enterprises.farmerNote: Forgiving of most things except low oxygen before dawn. In a hot, still week the risk is not the temperature itself but what warm water does to oxygen, and the loss happens overnight. A simple paddlewheel pays for itself the first time it is needed.
sourceReferences: FAO Cultured Aquatic Species Information Programme: Oreochromis niloticus

requirements.notes: Filling and topping up has to come from somewhere; a long lift is a permanent pumping bill.
A flood does not damage a pond, it empties it: the whole stock leaves over the bund in one night.

Built-up land and open water are excluded permanently. Tree cover is NOT excluded: MODIS at 500 m cannot tell an established plantation from intact forest, and 94% of this district reads as tree canopy, so excluding it would mark almost everywhere permanently unsuitable. Cells under canopy are flagged for a ground check instead.
Peat bunds slump and the water turns acid and tea-coloured.
Evaporation and seepage continue through a dry spell whether or not there is water to replace them.
Every extra degree of slope multiplies the earth that must be moved to get a level pond floor.
Below about 20% clay an earthen pond leaks faster than rain and inflow can refill it.
Acid pond soil suppresses natural productivity; agricultural lime is the standard fix.
Hot humid air means warm water, and warm water carries less dissolved oxygen. This, not air temperature, is what kills a pond overnight.
Growth stops below 20 C; mortality rises sharply below 14 C.

enterprises.name: African catfish
enterprises.description: Air-breathing catfish that tolerates water no other species will accept. The lowest-risk entry point into aquaculture.
enterprises.farmerNote: Keli gulps air at the surface, so the oxygen crash that wipes out a tilapia pond barely troubles it. That tolerance makes it the sensible first species on a marginal site, or a hedge where power for aeration is unreliable.
sourceReferences: FAO Cultured Aquatic Species Information Programme: Clarias gariepinus

Accessory air breathing makes low dissolved oxygen a much smaller risk.

enterprises.name: Striped catfish
enterprises.description: Fast-growing river catfish suited to deeper ponds and cages. Strong regional market and good feed conversion.
enterprises.farmerNote: Wants more depth than tilapia and does best where water can be exchanged, so a riverside site suits it. Grows quickly, but the feed bill is real and needs planning before stocking.
sourceReferences: FAO Cultured Aquatic Species Information Programme: Pangasianodon hypophthalmus

enterprises.name: Giant freshwater prawn
enterprises.description: High-value freshwater prawn for the premium local market. Lower yield per hectare than finfish but a far better price.
enterprises.farmerNote: The best price of anything you can put in a pond, and the least forgiving. Prawns need clean, well-oxygenated water and plenty of shelter on the bottom, and they will not tolerate the swings that keli shrugs off. Start small.
sourceReferences: FAO Cultured Aquatic Species Information Programme: Macrobrachium rosenbergii
New (2002), Farming Freshwater Prawns, FAO Fisheries Technical Paper 428

Moulting needs calcium, so soft acid water is a direct constraint on growth.
The least tolerant species here of the low dissolved oxygen that follows hot humid weather.
A narrow optimum; growth almost stops below 24 C.

enterprises.name: Broiler chicken
enterprises.description: Housed meat chickens on a 35-45 day cycle. The fastest turnover of any enterprise here and the most sensitive to heat.
enterprises.farmerNote: Birds cannot sweat; they lose heat by panting, and panting stops working when the air is already saturated. A humid, still afternoon late in the cycle, when the birds are heaviest, is when a shed is lost. Open sides and ridge ventilation matter more than the thermometer suggests.
sourceReferences: NRC (1971), A Guide to Environmental Research on Animals

requirements.notes: Daily water demand does not pause for a dry spell.
Livestock cannot be evacuated quickly. A flood that reaches the shed floor is a total loss.
Humidity is what disables evaporative cooling; it is not a secondary factor.
Housing, feed delivery and manure handling all need reasonably level ground.
A yard that never dries out means permanent foot and hygiene problems.
Above THI 76 feed intake falls and mortality climbs in the final week.

enterprises.name: Laying hen
enterprises.description: Egg production over a 70-80 week laying cycle. Steadier cash flow than broilers and a longer commitment.
enterprises.farmerNote: Income arrives daily rather than in a lump at the end of a cycle, which suits a household budget. Heat shows up as thin shells and dropped lay rather than dead birds, so the damage is easy to miss until the tray count falls.

requirements.notes: Daily water demand does not pause for a dry spell.
Livestock cannot be evacuated quickly. A flood that reaches the shed floor is a total loss.
Housing, feed delivery and manure handling all need reasonably level ground.
A yard that never dries out means permanent foot and hygiene problems.
Shell quality degrades before lay rate does, so heat stress is often detected late.

enterprises.name: Duck
enterprises.description: Hardy waterfowl for meat and eggs. Suits wet ground that would be a liability for any other animal.
enterprises.farmerNote: The obvious answer for the damp corner of a holding, and a natural partner for a fish pond or a paddy field after harvest. Far more tolerant of wet and heat than chickens, and cheaper to house.

requirements.notes: Open water is close to a requirement rather than a convenience.
Wet ground that would cause foot rot in goats is unremarkable for ducks.
Access to water for bathing gives ducks a cooling route poultry lack.

enterprises.name: Goat
enterprises.description: Browsing small ruminant for meat. Works on slopes and rough ground that no crop would justify clearing.
enterprises.farmerNote: Goats earn their keep on land that is too steep or too poor to plant, but they hate standing wet. Foot rot and internal parasites are the two things that ruin a herd here, and both come from permanently damp ground. Raised slatted housing is close to essential in this climate.
sourceReferences: NRC (2007), Nutrient Requirements of Small Ruminants

requirements.notes: Persistent wet drives foot rot and parasite burden; this climate is at the limit for goats kept on the ground.
Browsing stock use ground too steep to crop.

enterprises.name: Beef cattle
enterprises.description: Zebu-type beef cattle, often integrated under oil palm where the fallen fronds and ground cover provide grazing.
enterprises.farmerNote: Cattle under palm is a genuinely good pairing: the animals get shade and forage, the plantation gets weeding and manure. Zebu breeds handle this heat far better than European ones, but even they stop gaining weight when the index climbs, and the loss is invisible until weighing day.
sourceReferences: NRC (1971), A Guide to Environmental Research on Animals
Hahn (1999), Dynamic responses of cattle to thermal heat loads

requirements.notes: Daily water demand does not pause for a dry spell.
Livestock cannot be evacuated quickly. A flood that reaches the shed floor is a total loss.
Enough rain for year-round forage, but not so much that pasture becomes a quagmire.
Housing, feed delivery and manure handling all need reasonably level ground.
Heavy stock compact soft wet soil quickly, which then stops growing grass.
A yard that never dries out means permanent foot and hygiene problems.
Above THI 78 intake and weight gain fall; above 82 is the recognised danger band even for heat-adapted Bos indicus.

interventions.name: Contour bunds
interventions.description: Low earth ridges along the contour that intercept runoff and hold it long enough to infiltrate.
interventions.howItWorks: A cheaper alternative to terracing for annual crops on moderate slopes. Reduces soil loss and increases infiltration, but does not make the ground level or mechanisable.

interventions.name: Drip irrigation
interventions.description: Low-pressure emitters delivering water to the root zone on a schedule set by crop demand.
interventions.howItWorks: Covers the gap between rainfall and crop water requirement during dry spells, at roughly half the water a sprinkler would use. Needs a reliable source, so it usually pairs with a storage pond rather than replacing one.

interventions.name: Farm water storage pond
interventions.description: An excavated or embanked pond sized to carry the enterprise through the design dry spell.
interventions.howItWorks: Volume is the crop or stock water demand over the dry spell, less effective rainfall, plus evaporation and seepage losses over the same period. Sizing uses ET0 from the climate record and the 90th-percentile dry spell rather than the average one, because the pond only matters in a bad year.
sourceReferences: FAO, Manual on small earth dams (2010)

interventions.name: Field drainage
interventions.description: A network of field and collector drains sized to carry the design storm off the block within the period the crop can tolerate standing water.
interventions.howItWorks: Open drains intercept surface runoff and lower the water table between them. Spacing comes from the Hooghoudt equation using the soil hydraulic conductivity, the drain depth and the depth to the impermeable layer; depth and gradient come from the design rainfall and the crop's waterlogging tolerance.
sourceReferences: Ritzema (1994), Drainage Principles and Applications, ILRI Publication 16
FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 62, Guidelines for drainage design

interventions.name: Gravity irrigation channel
interventions.description: An open channel conveying water from a river or scheme offtake to the field by gravity.
interventions.howItWorks: The traditional answer for paddy where a source sits above the field. No pumping cost, but it depends on the source holding up through the dry months, which the climate record can check.

interventions.name: Land levelling
interventions.description: Cut-and-fill earthworks to bring a block to a uniform grade.
interventions.howItWorks: Required before a paddy basin or a pond can be built. Earthwork volume rises steeply with the starting slope, which is why a gentle site is so much cheaper to develop than a moderate one.
sourceReferences: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 45, Guidelines for designing and evaluating surface irrigation systems

interventions.name: Liming
interventions.description: Ground limestone or dolomite worked into the topsoil to raise pH and displace exchangeable aluminium.
interventions.howItWorks: Rate is calculated from the current pH, the target pH and the soil buffering capacity indicated by CEC and clay content. On the strongly acid soils common here this is usually the cheapest single intervention per unit of yield gained.
sourceReferences: FAO Soils Bulletin 55, Management of acid soils

interventions.name: Organic matter addition
interventions.description: Compost, manure, empty fruit bunch mulch or a cover crop, incorporated or surface applied.
interventions.howItWorks: Raises organic carbon, which improves aggregate stability, water holding capacity and nutrient retention together. The slowest intervention to show results and the one with the most durable effect.
sourceReferences: FAO, Soil organic carbon: the hidden potential (2017)

interventions.name: Perimeter bund
interventions.description: An earth embankment around the holding, built to the design flood level plus freeboard, with a controlled outlet.
interventions.howItWorks: Keeps external flood water out rather than moving internal water away. Height comes from the flood depth with a return period matched to the value at risk, plus 0.3-0.5 m of freeboard; the outlet must be gated or the bund simply traps rainfall inside.

interventions.name: Pond aeration
interventions.description: Paddlewheel or diffused-air aeration sized to the stocking density and the worst-case overnight oxygen demand.
interventions.howItWorks: Dissolved oxygen falls through the night and reaches its minimum just before dawn, and warm water holds less of it to begin with. Aeration covers that window. Sized from standing stock, water temperature and pond volume.
sourceReferences: Boyd (1998), Pond water aeration systems, Aquacultural Engineering 18

interventions.name: Pond liming
interventions.description: Agricultural lime applied to the pond bottom and water to raise alkalinity and pH.
interventions.howItWorks: Acid pond soils, common on the peat-influenced soils here, suppress natural food production and stress stock. Liming buffers pH swings and improves the response to fertilisation.
sourceReferences: Boyd & Tucker (1998), Pond Aquaculture Water Quality Management

interventions.name: Pond lining
interventions.description: HDPE membrane or a compacted clay blanket to stop seepage from a pond on permeable ground.
interventions.howItWorks: Makes aquaculture possible on sandy sites that would otherwise lose more water than can be replaced. A significant capital cost that should be weighed against simply choosing a clay site.

interventions.name: Rain shelter
interventions.description: A simple roofed structure over a vegetable bed, open at the sides.
interventions.howItWorks: Keeps leaves dry without trapping heat, which cuts foliar disease sharply in a wet climate and prevents fruit splitting. Usually the difference between a viable and an unviable tomato crop in the humid lowlands.
sourceReferences: FAO, Good Agricultural Practices for greenhouse vegetable crops (2013)

interventions.name: Raised beds
interventions.description: Planting beds lifted above the surrounding ground with furrows between them, so the root zone stays above the water table even when the field is saturated.
interventions.howItWorks: Raising the root zone by 30-60 cm removes the waterlogging that causes root rot, without needing to drain the whole block. The cheapest effective answer for high-value shallow-rooted crops on flat, poorly drained ground.
sourceReferences: FAO, Good Agricultural Practices for horticulture in the humid tropics

interventions.name: Raised slatted housing
interventions.description: Slatted floor housing raised above the ground, with manure falling through for separate collection.
interventions.howItWorks: The standard answer for small ruminants in a wet tropical climate. Keeps feet dry, breaks the parasite cycle between animal and ground, and improves air flow under the animals.
sourceReferences: FAO, Small ruminant housing in the humid tropics

interventions.name: Shade and ventilation
interventions.description: Shade structures, open-sided housing with ridge ventilation, and in severe cases evaporative cooling or sprinklers.
interventions.howItWorks: Cuts the radiant heat load and restores air movement so animals can shed heat. In humid air, air movement matters more than misting, because evaporative cooling is already close to saturated.
sourceReferences: FAO, Shelter and housing for livestock in hot climates

interventions.name: Terracing
interventions.description: Bench or contour terraces cut across the slope to shorten slope length and slow runoff.
interventions.howItWorks: Converts a continuous slope into a series of near-level benches, cutting erosion sharply and making the ground workable. Expensive to build and only justified for a perennial crop that will occupy the land for decades.

interventions.name: Peat water-table control
interventions.description: Weirs and gated outlets holding the water table in a drained peat block within a narrow band, typically 40-60 cm below the surface.
interventions.howItWorks: Deep drainage of peat causes irreversible subsidence of roughly 5 cm a year and large carbon loss. Holding the table high enough to limit oxidation, but low enough for roots, is the difference between a 25-year stand and a field that drops below the drain in a decade.
sourceReferences: Wosten et al. (1997), Peat subsidence and its practical implications

interventions.name: Windbreak planting
interventions.description: Rows of fast-growing trees across the prevailing wind, protecting roughly ten times their height downwind.
interventions.howItWorks: Reduces wind speed and mechanical damage, and lowers evaporative demand behind the belt. Slow to establish, so it is planted with the crop rather than after the first loss.
sourceReferences: FAO Conservation Guide 15, Windbreaks and shelterbelts

categories.label: Perennial crops
categories.examples: Oil palm, coconut, rubber, pepper, durian, cocoa
categories.description: Planted once and harvested for decades. The ground you choose is a 25-year commitment, so this is the category where a 2050 climate projection genuinely changes the decision.

categories.label: Seasonal crops
categories.description: One or two crops a year tied to the rains. The decision that matters is when to plant and whether the wet window is shifting.

categories.label: Short-cycle crops
categories.examples: Kangkung, sawi, tomato, chilli, cucumber, long bean
categories.description: Harvested in weeks. Low commitment and the natural fit for rotation, cash flow and recovering soil between heavier crops.

categories.label: Aquaculture
categories.examples: Tilapia, keli, patin, freshwater prawn, brackish shrimp
categories.description: Ponds and cages. Fish are more exposed to weather than most farmers expect: a heat wave strips oxygen out of the water, and a drought turns pond top-up into a cost you cannot avoid.

categories.label: Livestock
categories.description: Animals need shade, water and feed every single day, so heat-stress days and dry-spell length bite harder here than annual averages suggest.
